To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Hydration of the SC induces reversible changes of the impedance properties of excised skin membranes, 2) the changes are mainly due to changes in the dynamics and organization of the SC keratin filament terminals, 3) the SC lipid organization is unaffected by hydration, but the dynamics of the fluid lipid fraction changes, and 4) the changes in dynamics of the SC components can explain the observed changes of the impedance.
the skin membrane impedance is sensitive to the water activity gradient and the impedance response is correlated with the molecular properties of the skin membrane.
hydration of the SC induces reversible changes in the impedance properties and that these changes can be explained in terms of the molecular structure of the skin components.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the skin barrier and how it can be modulated to increase drug delivery.
the development of a fundamental understanding of how skin membrane properties are affected by hydration, which is a prerequisite for the development of improved transdermal drug delivery systems.
the molecular and macroscopic effects of hydration on the SC and the effect of hydration state on the skin membrane impedance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
water in the SC is not just a simple plasticizer of the lipids and keratin, but also a key player in the dynamics of both components and in the organization of the SC.
hydration increases the permeability of the SC, but the molecular details are complex and require further studies.
hydration increases both the permeability of skin and the diffusivity of the permeating molecules.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effect of hydration is to increase the permeability by increasing the fluid lipid fraction and the mobility of the keratin filaments.
the SC lipids are the most important components that control skin permeability, whereas the keratin is the most important component for maintaining the structural integrity of the SC.

the hydration of the SC lipids is the key factor in the permeability barrier function of skin, as the hydration of the lipid phase induces a change of the lipid packing and dynamics, which in turn affects the permeability.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hydration affects the SC in a complex fashion, and that the effect is dependent on both the hydration state and the water gradient.

the impedance response of skin is highly dependent on the state of hydration of the SC, and that this is a consequence of a combination of changes in the properties of both the lipid and keratin SC components.
the effect of hydration is not only to increase the amount of water in the SC but also to change the dynamics of the SC components.
